Use an N95 mask or limit your exposure to smoke.
If not evacuating, shelter indoors where smoke levels are lower.

after.text: Do not return home until authorities say it is safe.
Avoid hot ash, charred trees, smoldering debris and live embers.
Use a respirator and wet debris to limit breathing dust.
Text or use social media to reach family; call only in emergencies.

before.text: Make conserving water a part of your daily life.
Check plumbing for leaks and have them repaired.
Never pour away water that could be reused, such as for plants.

Stay out of damaged buildings; wear sturdy shoes in storm debris.

before.text: Learn to recognize the signs of heat illnesses.

Do not rely on a fan as your primary cooling device.
Cover windows with drapes or shades.

during.text: Never leave people or pets in a closed car.
No air conditioning at home? Go to a cooling center.
Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated.
Avoid high-energy activities and outdoor work during midday heat.

after.text: Heat stroke is an emergency: call emergency services or go to hospital.

after.text: Move heat stroke victims to cool shade and apply cold, wet cloths.
With heat cramps or exhaustion, go somewhere cooler and sip water.

before.text: Make a household plan, including pets, for where to go.
Leave if told to evacuate or if staying home feels unsafe.
Near a wildfire burn area, get alerts and watch weather forecasts.
Listen and watch for rushing water, mud or unusual sounds.

during.text: Stay alert and awake in storms; many landslide deaths happen during sleep.
In a landslide's path, move uphill as quickly as possible.
Never cross a road with water or mud flowing.
Near streams, watch for sudden flow changes or water turning muddy.

after.text: Stay away from the slide area; more slides may follow.
Watch for flooding, which sometimes follows landslides and debris flows.
Check for injured or trapped people without entering the slide; direct rescuers.
Report broken utility lines and damaged roads or railways to authorities.

after.text: Know the signs of hypothermia and how to treat it.
Get to a warm shelter; warm the center of the body first.
Treat a body temperature below 95°F (35°C) as an emergency.
Feeling anxious is normal; talk to someone if you are upset.

before.text: Build an emergency kit.

during.text: Keep electricity use as low as possible to help avoid blackouts.
Follow the instructions given in official emergency alerts.
Disconnect electrical appliances if local officials instruct you to.
Avoid phone calls unless absolutely necessary; keep lines open for responders.

after.text: Throw away food held at 40°F (4°C) or higher for 2+ hours.
Never judge food safety by taste, look or smell.

Power out over a day? Discard refrigerated medicine unless labeled otherwise.

before.text: Plan how your family will reconnect and where you will meet.

during.text: Stay informed and follow the instructions of local authorities.

When sheltering in place, use an interior room with few windows.

after.text: Return home only when local officials say it is safe.
